tools.name: get_experience
tools.title: Get Edwin Jorge's (edgeorgie) real work experience
tools.description: Returns the candidate's actual work history exactly as written on his resume (resume.txt) — employer, title, dates, and bullets, verbatim, no embellishment. Covers Mercado Libre (Software Engineer, Nov 2022-present, AI workflows/agent-based architectures at 4.3M+ LATAM users), Vansa, and Freelance roles.

tools.name: get_projects
tools.title: Get Edwin Jorge's (edgeorgie) real shipped project evidence
tools.description: Returns the 6 publicly shipped artifacts (triage-desk, eval-lab, repoask-mcp, crispy-profiling, simplescope, agentlens) with their real measured metrics, PR/commit/run URLs, and live demo links — sourced from each repo's public commit history and RELIABILITY-REPORT.md. No metric here is estimated or invented; every claim cites exactly where it was verified. EVERY project also returns a non-empty `limitations` array stating caveats a caller could not infer from its metrics (no adoption, not on a registry, a self-labeled benchmark, a missing licence, a capability it deliberately lacks). Caveats are mandatory per entry, not added only where they happened to be noticed, so an absent caveat never means 'this one has none'.

tools.name: get_story
tools.title: Get Edwin Jorge's (edgeorgie) personal story as a timeline
tools.description: Returns a chronological, beat-by-beat narrative of who the candidate is beyond the resume — from shipping a solo 2D platformer at 15, through his Electronic Engineering + Software degrees, picking up Kotlin/Swift on the job, owning UX/design decisions, to what he's self-teaching right now (Unreal Engine game dev, guitar, a 4x/week morning gym routine). Structured as ordered beats (year, label, body), not a single prose block — render it as an actual timeline rather than dumping the text. Unlike ask_about_edgeorgie, this tool does NOT do retrieval and returns no line-level citations: the beats are the candidate's own hand-written summary, maintained as editorial copy in src/engine.ts. The underlying facts also appear in data/RECRUITER-FAQ.md and some phrasing overlaps with it, so treat this as editorial copy rather than either a quote or a clean paraphrase — use ask_about_edgeorgie when you need a cited source file and line range.

tools.name: ask_about_edgeorgie
tools.title: Ask a grounded, cited question about Edwin Jorge (edgeorgie)
tools.description: Answers a natural-language question about the candidate's experience, projects, or skills using TF-IDF retrieval over a corpus built ONLY from his real resume.txt, RELIABILITY-REPORT.md, BUILD-LOG.md, and RECRUITER-FAQ.md (public evidence only). Returns citations with exact source file + line range. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY is set, also returns a synthesized prose answer with inline [n] citations grounded strictly in the retrieved excerpts; otherwise 'answer' is a deterministic citation dump and 'answerMode' is 'deterministic'. If a key is set but the provider call fails, 'answerMode' is 'synthesis-failed' (not 'deterministic') and 'llmKeyConfigured' is true, so the cause is never misreported as a missing key. Never answers beyond what's indexed — if nothing relevant is found, it says so rather than inventing an answer.

topK.description: Number of citations to return. Default 6.

content.text:
Software Engineer focused on AI-enabled full-stack development with 5+ years of experience building scalable web platforms using TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Node.js. Dual degrees in Electronic Engineering and Software Development. Contributed to applications serving 4.3M+ users across LATAM, delivering high-performance and intelligent digital experiences.

Mercado Libre — Software Engineer (November 2022 – present)
  - Designed AI workflows and agent-based architectures, defining agent rules, skills, and orchestration across services.
  - Using that agentic-architecture workflow, delivered 10+ initiatives end-to-end solo (100% individually owned), 5 of them directly monetizable and the rest product-improvement initiatives, together reaching 4M+ users across LATAM.
  - Led those initiatives directly, owning scope, delivery, and cross-team coordination end-to-end.
  - Led cross-platform initiatives (web, mobile, TV/Samsung/LG) using Spec-Driven Development and scalable frontend architecture.
  - Worked across platforms beyond desktop web: mobile WebViews and AI-assisted native development for Android (Kotlin) and iOS (Swift).
  - Shipped a production feature used by 1.5M+ users, delivered in record time with zero production incidents.
  - Built stateful and stateless React components with TypeScript, improving performance and maintainability.
  - Implemented observability and monitoring using Kibana, NewRelic, Datadog, and Grafana aligned with SRE practices (SLA/SLI/SLO).
  - Applied Clean Architecture and Domain-Driven Design (DDD) while refactoring legacy systems and improving code quality.
  - Developed robust APIs with caching, idempotency, and low-latency performance.
  - Implemented comprehensive testing (Unit, Integration, E2E) and improved reliability across services.
  - Contributed to OTT video streaming platforms, including Chromecast Web Receiver development and smart TV web receivers for LG, Samsung (Tizen), Vidaa, and TitanOS.
  - Worked on advertising (ads) initiatives with measurable success.
  - Collaborated with engineering, product, and design teams to deliver scalable features and technical documentation.

Vansa — Front-end Developer (February 2022 – July 2022)
  - Built React-based frontend applications using JavaScript, SASS, and Framer Motion.
  - Developed responsive dashboards using HTML5 (JSX), CSS Grid, and modern UI patterns.
  - Optimized performance, accessibility (a11y), and cross-browser compatibility.
  - Applied Atomic Design, SOLID principles, and Clean Architecture to deliver reusable and maintainable components.

Freelance — Front-end Developer & UI/UX Designer (April 2020 – February 2022)
  - Designed frontend architecture and design systems for web applications.
  - Translated Figma UI/UX designs into scalable React interfaces with reusable components and hooks.
  - Implemented responsive UI using CSS/SASS (Grid, Flexbox, media queries) and animations with Framer Motion.
  - Improved Time to Interactive (TTI) using Next.js Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and SEO optimization.

content.text:
## triage-desk
GitHub-webhook-triggered autonomous triage bot (not a human-clicked UI demo). Fires on real `issues: [opened]` / `pull_request_target: [opened]` webhooks, posts a triage comment and applies kind/priority labels via Octokit using the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN. Falls back to a deterministic heuristic classifier when no LLM key is configured (truthfully labeled in each run, not faked as an LLM call).

Metrics:
- Webhook-triggered run (issue #26 opened -> bot commented + labeled) completed in 22s, conclusion: success
- Heuristic classifier accuracy: 83.3% (15/18) on both kind and priority, self-labeled ground truth, n=18 — see RELIABILITY-REPORT.md
- Duplicate detection: 1/2 (50%) — near-verbatim duplicate caught, paraphrased duplicate missed (Jaccard token-overlap limitation)
- 22/22 local unit tests passing
- eval-lab-gated CI: 6/6 cases passed (cross-dogfooded, see eval-lab entry below)

Limitations:
- 0 GitHub stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers — nobody but the author has used it. The webhook runs and the accuracy benchmark are real, the adoption is zero.
- The 83.3% accuracy figure is self-labeled ground truth on n=18 issues written by the same person who wrote the classifier. Treat it as an internal consistency check, not a benchmark.
- The classifier that produced those numbers is the deterministic HEURISTIC path, not an LLM — no LLM key is configured in the deployed workflow, so the LLM branch has never run against real traffic.
- Not published to any registry (`https://registry.npmjs.org/triage-desk` → 404). It runs as a GitHub Actions workflow in its own repo; using it elsewhere means copying the workflow.

## eval-lab
Installable CLI + reusable GitHub Action for evaluating prompts/agents (variant runner, deterministic checks, LLM judge, regression diff vs. a baseline). Dogfooded in its own CI and in triage-desk's CI (eval-lab gates triage-desk's real heuristic-triage logic). Ships an offline `demo` model so it runs at $0 cost with zero API key.

Metrics:
- Benchmark: 100% pass rate (24/24 cells), 3 runs, avg latency 20.21ms/cell, wall-clock ~255-259ms/run, $0 cost — see RELIABILITY-REPORT.md section 1
- 7/7 local unit tests passing (node:test)
- PR CI run caught a real regression: baseline run reported 'all 2 cells passed'; regressed run reported '1 regression(s), 0 fix(es)' and exited 1

Limitations:
- 0 GitHub stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers. The CI integration is real and cross-dogfooded into triage-desk, but no third party has adopted it.
- Not published to npm (`https://registry.npmjs.org/eval-lab` → 404, and the scoped `@edgeorgie/eval-lab` → 404 too). "Installable CLI" means installable from GitHub, not `npm i eval-lab`.
- The 100% / 24-of-24 benchmark runs entirely against the built-in offline `demo` model, which is deterministic by design. It measures that the harness, checks and regression diff work — it measures nothing about any real model's quality, and the $0 cost and ~20ms latency are properties of the stub, not of a live provider.
- The LLM-judge path exists but is not covered by the benchmark above, because running it needs a provider key that CI does not have.

## repoask-mcp
MCP server (official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) that lets an agent index any public GitHub repo and ask it questions, getting back TF-IDF-retrieved citations with exact file+line ranges (optional LLM synthesis layered on top). Ships both stdio and Streamable HTTP transports from one shared tool factory, plus a human-usable web UI backed by the identical engine. Deployed live and publicly reachable with no auth wall.

Metrics:
- 3/3 automated tests passing against real network calls to GitHub (no mocks)
- Live public URL verified with a bare unauthenticated curl: GET / -> 200 health JSON, no SSO redirect
- Real external MCP SDK Client (StreamableHTTPClientTransport) over the open internet: list_tools, index_repo(octocat/git-consortium) -> fileCount=2, chunkCount=8; ask_repo -> 4 real citations
- Vercel deployment debugging: 3 real root causes found and fixed (builds-vs-rewrites build-target detection, routes-vs-rewrites routing-mode mismatch once builds was added, ssoProtection deploymentProtection PATCHed off via the Vercel API) — this debugging story is documented start-to-finish in BUILD-LOG.md and progress.log

Limitations:
- 0 GitHub stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, not on npm (`https://registry.npmjs.org/repoask-mcp` → 404). Deployed and publicly callable is not the same as used by anyone.
- Retrieval is TF-IDF over chunked files — lexical, not semantic. A question that shares no vocabulary with the source returns weak or no citations, and there is no embedding model anywhere in the path.
- The deployed instance has no LLM key configured, so it answers in deterministic citation-only mode. The LLM synthesis layer is implemented but inert in production.
- The 3/3 test figure is three tests. It covers the real network path to GitHub with no mocks, which is the valuable part, but it is a smoke suite rather than broad coverage.
- No auth and no per-caller quota beyond a rate limit — anyone can make it index public repos on the author's deployment.

## crispy-profiling
React re-render profiler shipped as four surfaces off one engine: CLI, GitHub Action, MCP server, and an Agent Skill (skills/react-render-profiling/SKILL.md) so Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and similar tools can measure a re-render fix instead of guessing at one. Opens the target app in headless Chromium, drives described interactions, and reports which components re-rendered, how many times, why (props/state/context/parent), and which renders were avoidable. Published to npm.

Metrics:
- Published and installable: `npm i -D crispy-profiling` (https://www.npmjs.com/package/crispy-profiling)
- Validated against 5 real open-source apps (Redux Essentials, Next.js App Router Playground, Excalidraw, shadcn-admin, react-admin) — found a fixable re-render problem in each
- OpenSSF Scorecard badge live on the repo; CI badge live and green
- Tested on React 19, validated on 18.3 and 19.0 apps

Limitations:
- 0 GitHub stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers. It is published and installable, which is a real bar most of these do not clear, but published is not adopted.
- The download count is a lifetime total, not a rate: every npm download window wide enough to contain the first publish (2026-10-05) returns the same running total, so a last-week and a last-month figure read identically until the window rolls past that date. The figure is 1378 as of 2026-10-15, and it is dated because it moves — an earlier snapshot of 754 was still being served here days after npm had passed it. Every nonzero day lines up with the author's own publishes: 523 on Oct 5 (0.1.0, 0.2.0) and 512 on Oct 10 (0.4.0, 0.5.0 and 0.6.0 inside three hours), which is the shape of registry mirrors and CI refetching a new version, not users.
- The "found a fixable re-render problem in each of 5 apps" result was produced and judged by the author. No maintainer of those apps reviewed or accepted a fix.
- 0 open issues on the repo as of 2026-10-11, and the two that were open (both unresolved product work) have since been closed.

## simplescope
Interactive, visual, gamified platform for learning algorithms by watching real JavaScript run — not static diagrams. Built with Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript, Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui, MDX lessons; optional account/progress-sync via Better Auth + Drizzle on Neon Postgres, with the site fully functional with zero environment variables (progress falls back to browser localStorage) when accounts aren't configured.

Metrics:
- Deployed live and publicly reachable: https://simplescope-one.vercel.app
- Works with zero required env vars — graceful degradation design (accounts hide automatically, localStorage progress still works) verified from the repo's own README, not assumed

Limitations:
- It carries NO LICENCE FILE — the GitHub API reports `NOASSERTION`, the only one of these six artifacts that is not MIT. Legally that means default copyright: nobody may reuse, modify or redistribute it, including a reviewer who only wants to clone and run it. This is stated rather than silently fixed because choosing a licence is a commitment on the author's own work, not an automated edit.
- Its GitHub repo is PRIVATE, so none of its repo-state numbers can be verified by a reader: the API returns 404 unauthenticated, and the linked repo URL will not open for anyone but the author. Stated from the authenticated view on 2026-10-11: 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, 12 open issues — several of them unfinished product work (a Lighthouse audit, an SEO audit, per-page content gaps, a trademark/domain question), not stale noise. Unlike every other artifact here, those figures are maintained by hand and are not covered by this repo's automated freshness check, precisely because a private repo cannot be checked without a credential. The deployed site is public and returns 200.
- It is the only artifact here with no automated-test or accuracy metric of any kind. Its evidence is that it is deployed and that the zero-env-var degradation works; there is no measured number behind it.
- Not on npm and not intended to be — it is a deployed web app. Nothing here is installable or agent-callable; it is the one artifact aimed only at humans.

## agentlens
Zero-dependency tracing + waterfall visualizer for AI agent tool calls: latency, tokens, cost, nesting, errors. Built to answer 'which step of this agent run was slow, and which one threw' — `node:async_hooks` AsyncLocalStorage propagates parent/child span context without threading a context object through every signature, so concurrent sibling spans cannot leak into each other's parent. `renderHtml` emits a self-contained waterfall with no external references.

Metrics:
- Zero runtime dependencies — only two Node builtins (`node:async_hooks`, `node:crypto`), Node 18+
- 5/5 tests passing on a fresh clone (tests 5 / pass 5 / fail 0)
- 6/6 GitHub Actions CI runs `success`
- Viewer deployed live and publicly reachable: https://agentlens-nine.vercel.app/ returns 200

Limitations:
- Does NOT call any LLM API and knows no provider's pricing — `tokensIn`/`tokensOut`/`costUsd`/`model` are optional fields the caller sets via `setAttrs()`, and agentlens only sums what it is told. The demo's token numbers are stubbed and labeled as demo values so the demo costs nothing and needs no API key.
- NOT published on the npm registry, for two independent reasons: no npm credentials in the build environment (`npm whoami` -> ENEEDAUTH), and the name `agentlens` is already taken on npm by an unrelated package, so publishing would require renaming (e.g. `@edgeorgie/agentlens`). Installing from GitHub works today: `npm install github:edgeorgie/agentlens`.
- Version 0.1.0, 0 stars, no known users — a tool built for the author's own use that has not been adopted by anyone.

It means an agent is a real user of the thing, not an afterthought bolted onto a human UI. I've been building this way since the first models that were actually good enough to build on — at Mercado Libre on production agent workflows, and in my own projects to try things I couldn't try at work.

Three things I've landed on:

**The harness matters more than the prompt.** Most of the real engineering is the control architecture around the model: which tools exist, what the agent is allowed to do, where failures get caught, how output gets verified before anyone trusts it. Prompts are the easy part, and the part people obsess over.

---

[2] BUILD-LOG.md (lines 35-40):
The newest of these is `agentlens` ([repo](https://github.com/edgeorgie/agentlens)) — "zero-dependency tracing + waterfall visualizer for AI agent tool calls: latency, tokens, cost, nesting, errors." It came out of a plain annoyance: when a multi-step agent run goes wrong, I couldn't see *where*. Which tool call was slow, which one threw, what was nested under what. So I wrote the smallest thing that would answer that.

It's version 0.1.0 and it has no runtime dependencies at all — only two Node builtins, `node:async_hooks` and `node:crypto`, on Node 18+. `AsyncLocalStorage` is doing the interesting work: it's what lets a span know its own parent without me threading a context object through every function signature, and it's what makes concurrent sibling spans not leak into each other's parent. There are 5 tests and all 5 pass on a fresh clone (`tests 5 / pass 5 / fail 0`): nested spans getting the right parent/child via AsyncLocalStorage, a span whose fn throws recording error status and message without losing the rest of the trace, token and cost fields summing into trace totals, concurrent siblings not cross-contaminating parent context, and `renderHtml` producing self-contained HTML with no external references. CI is 6 GitHub Actions runs, all 6 `success`. The viewer is live at `https://agentlens-nine.vercel.app/` (200). `npm run demo` runs a small multi-step agent — plan -> search_docs -> read_doc x2 -> write_summary — where one of the read steps deliberately fails, because an error path you've never rendered is an error path you don't know renders.

Two limitations. First: agentlens does not call any LLM API and does not know any provider's pricing. Tokens and cost are optional fields the caller sets themselves via `setAttrs({ tokensIn, tokensOut, costUsd, model })`, and agentlens only sums what it's told — the demo's token numbers are stubbed and labeled as demo values, specifically so the demo costs nothing and needs no API key. If you want real cost, you supply real cost. Second: it is not published on the npm registry. Two separate reasons, not one — there are no npm credentials in this build environment (`npm whoami` returns `ENEEDAUTH`), and independently of that the name `agentlens` is already taken on npm by an unrelated package, so publishing would mean renaming to something like `@edgeorgie/agentlens`. Installing from GitHub works today: `npm install github:edgeorgie/agentlens`. It has 0 stars and no users I know of; it's a tool I built for myself and it hasn't been adopted by anyone.

---

[3] RECRUITER-FAQ.md (lines 65-70):
JavaScript/TypeScript is my core expertise — that's where I'm deepest and fastest. I don't shy away from new stacks though: at Mercado Libre I did AI-assisted native development in Kotlin (Android) and Swift (iOS) alongside the web work, picking both up on the job rather than coming in already fluent. I'm self-taught by background — I hold an Electronic Engineering degree alongside Software Development, and most of what I know about AI/agentic systems specifically I taught myself outside of any formal course.

## Do you design, or just build to someone else's design?

Both. UX and interaction design are something I actively work on, not just hand off — the projects I've shipped (this portfolio included) are my own design decisions, not a template. I care about how something feels to use, not just whether the API underneath is correct.

---

Both. UX and interaction design are something I actively work on, not just hand off — the projects I've shipped (this portfolio included) are my own design decisions, not a template. I care about how something feels to use, not just whether the API underneath is correct.

# Build log: triage-desk, eval-lab, repoask-mcp, crispy-profiling, simplescope, agentlens

*Posted 2026-10-09, updated 2026-10-11 (agentlens added, the repoask-mcp deployment section corrected once it actually shipped, and crispy-profiling + simplescope written up after my own MCP server reported it had no information about them). Working notes from converting side projects from "demo I click through" into "thing an agent or CI pipeline actually drives." Writing this the way I'd want to read it — including the parts that didn't work on the first try.*

I keep a progress log while I work (mostly for myself, partly so I don't quietly round a "mostly works" into a "it works"). This is the cleaned-up version of a few days from that log, covering the six things I've actually shipped: a webhook-triggered GitHub triage bot, an eval CLI/Action, a fresh MCP server built off an older RAG side project, a React re-render profiler published to npm, an interactive algorithms-learning site, and a tracer for watching my own agents run. I'm not going to pretend any of this went in a straight line.

What it can't do, stated upfront: it does not call any LLM API and doesn't know any provider's pricing — tokens and cost are optional fields you set yourself via `setAttrs({ tokensIn, tokensOut, costUsd, model })` and agentlens only sums what you tell it, so the demo's token numbers are stubbed demo values (that's deliberate, it keeps the demo free and key-less). It's also not on the npm registry: there are no npm credentials in my build environment (`npm whoami` returns ENEEDAUTH), and separately the name `agentlens` is already taken on npm by an unrelated package, so publishing means renaming to something like `@edgeorgie/agentlens`. `npm install github:edgeorgie/agentlens` works today. It has 0 stars and no users — I built it for my own debugging, not for an audience.

## What's your core technical stack, and how comfortable are you picking up a new one?

JavaScript/TypeScript is my core expertise — that's where I'm deepest and fastest. I don't shy away from new stacks though: at Mercado Libre I did AI-assisted native development in Kotlin (Android) and Swift (iOS) alongside the web work, picking both up on the job rather than coming in already fluent. I'm self-taught by background — I hold an Electronic Engineering degree alongside Software Development, and most of what I know about AI/agentic systems specifically I taught myself outside of any formal course.

The last piece worth writing up: I benchmarked triage-desk's fallback heuristic (the path that runs when no LLM key is configured) against 18 self-labeled synthetic issues. 83.3% (15/18) on both `kind` and `priority` classification, same three misses for both since they're coupled. I expected something cleaner. The actual confusion matrix is more interesting than the number: one issue titled "...or a bug?" got classified as a bug purely because the literal substring "bug" appears before the question-detection branch runs in the if/else chain — a rhetorical mention of the word outranks the actual question structure. A paraphrased duplicate issue was missed entirely by the Jaccard token-overlap duplicate detector, while a near-verbatim duplicate was caught — the detector is brittle to rewording, not just noise-sensitive. None of this is a "needs more training data" problem, it's a few lines of ordering and a weak similarity metric. Worth fixing, but the number and failure modes here are reported as measured, not rounded up. ([ACCURACY.md](https://github.com/edgeorgie/triage-desk/blob/main/ACCURACY.md), [PR #28](https://github.com/edgeorgie/triage-desk/pull/28))
